cells.tense: The sorting is happening now, and the pen is in your hand.
cells.ask: Name what the closing is for, then take the first step you can do today.
cells.core:
You can hold what's tangled up here without forcing a neat order onto it. The loose ends, the old obligation, the thing that mattered once and doesn't now — you can see each one clearly, and you know which still has weight. That's the whole work. Nothing's being bulldozed.

When you end something here, you know what it's for. You put the pieces down in an order that holds and let the rest go on purpose — not perfectly, just cleanly enough. Fairness runs through it too: what you keep, what you release, who gets told. That's what made this work in the first place, and it's free to keep feeding what comes next.

cells.tense: You'll have the whole ending scripted out in advance, bracing for a future you can't write in.
cells.ask: Say the date out loud, then let the rest stay unplanned until that day.
cells.core:
You've already run the whole scene. What you'll say, how they'll take it, what it means six months later — the plan has gotten so much rehearsal that the ending itself stays put. You keep gathering the loose ends into a smarter order, and the pile just gets better organized.

That's the bend: planning the closing has replaced doing it. The thing you're trying to leave is still in the room, and each day of holding adds a reason not to move. Direction comes back by feeling your way into one actual step instead of mapping the whole route. Pick the day. Do one thing. Let the feeling that you're leaving something real set the direction, not the script.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that's already behind you, and the ending is still undone.
cells.ask: Sit with one thing you're still quietly holding, and let one person close to you hear why it matters.
cells.core:
The clearing here hasn't started. Things that needed ending are still sitting in place, and putting them in the open means saying who and what and why — so it doesn't happen. Gathering your thoughts into one order takes energy, and that energy isn't there right now. So the loose ends stay scattered and the room stays full.

The work isn't to force an ending this week. It's the smaller thing: let what you already feel about this be felt, with someone who doesn't need it fixed. Sitting with what's known, before asking it to move — that's where a person comes back from. Once that's real, the rest can start on its own.

cells.tense: You already ended it in how you live, and you're telling it as if it just happened.
cells.ask: Tell one person the truth about what you already finished, and celebrate that with them.
cells.core:
You've been moving as if the old thing were behind you — you stopped carrying it through your week, stopped planning around it, changed what you do without announcing anything. The ending is running. What's missing is the saying.

That's the bend: the choice got filed under circumstance. People hear it framed as what just happened to you, and you go along, which is a quieter way of taking no credit for a hard call you made. The way back is to say it plainly and let it be worth something — tell someone, let them mark it with you. The call was yours. Naming it in front of people is how it becomes yours all the way.
